For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kathina is one that is terminated by the passing of the time limit.

With the robe completed, thinking, 'I will return, I will return,' he arrives in time for the withdrawal of the kathina. For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kathina occurs together with the other bhikkhus.

Chakkaṃ.

The Hexad is finished.

Vippakatasamādāyapannarasakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Fifteen Cases Concerning Properly Taking an Unfinished Robe is finished.

Ādāyabhāṇavāro.

The Section on Taking

195. Anāsādoḷasakaṃ

The Twelve Cases of No Expectation

318. Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Anāsāya labhati, āsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

318. A bhikkhu, having participated in the spreading of the kathina, departs with the expectation of a robe. Having gone outside the boundary, he pursues that prospect of a robe. He obtains it from an unexpected source; he does not obtain it from the expected source. The thought occurs to him: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' He has that robe made. For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kathina is one finalized by completion.

196. Āsādoḷasakaṃ

196. The Twelve Cases of Expectation

319. Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So [T 2.0152] bahisīmagato [V 0.0344] taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

319. A bhikkhu, having participated in the spreading of the kathina, departs with the expectation of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he pursues that prospect of a robe. He obtains it from an expected source; he does not obtain it from an unexpected source. The thought occurs to him: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' He has that robe made. For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kathina is one finalized by completion.

Bhikkhu [M 0.0365] atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. To him, this thought occurs: 'I will not have this robe made, nor will I return.' For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with his decision.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. To him, this thought occurs: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' He has that robe made. While that robe is being made for him, it is lost. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the loss.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. Tassa bahisīmagatassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsissaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Tassa sā cīvarāsā upacchijjati. Tassa bhikkhuno āsāvacchediko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' To him, having gone outside the boundary, this thought occurs: 'I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here, and I will not return.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. For him, that hope for a robe is cut off. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is the cutting off of hope.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato suṇāti – “ubbhataṃ kira [P 1.0261] tasmiṃ āvāse kathina”nti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “yato tasmiṃ āvāse ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ, idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsissa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati[T 2.0153], anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he hears, 'It is said that the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery.' To him, this thought occurs: 'Since the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery, I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. To him, this thought occurs: 'I will have this robe made right here, and I will not return.' He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the completion.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato suṇāti – “ubbhataṃ kira tasmiṃ āvāse kathina”nti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “yato tasmiṃ āvāse ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ, idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsissa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A bhikkhu for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with hope for a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he hears, 'It is said that the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery.' To him, this thought occurs: 'Since the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery, I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. To him, this thought occurs: 'I will not have this robe made, nor will I return.' For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with his decision.

Bhikkhu [V 0.0345] atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato suṇāti – “ubbhataṃ kira tasmiṃ āvāse kathina”nti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “yato tasmiṃ āvāse ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ, idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ [M 0.0366] payirupāsissa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A bhikkhu for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with hope for a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he hears, 'It is said that the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery.' To him, this thought occurs: 'Since the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery, I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. To him, this thought occurs: 'I will have this robe made right here, and I will not return.' He has that robe made. For him, that robe is lost while it is being made. For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the loss.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato suṇāti – “ubbhataṃ kira tasmiṃ āvāse kathina”nti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “yato tasmiṃ āvāse ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ, idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsissaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Tassa sā cīvarāsā upacchijjati. Tassa [T 2.0154] bhikkhuno āsāvacchediko kathinuddhāro.

A bhikkhu for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with hope for a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he hears, 'It is said that the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery.' To him, this thought occurs: 'Since the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery, I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here, and I will not return.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. For that bhikkhu, that hope for a robe is cut off. For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is the cutting off of hope.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. So katacīvaro suṇāti – “ubbhataṃ kira tasmiṃ āvāse kathina”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno savanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A bhikkhu for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with hope for a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. He has that robe made. Having a completed robe, he hears, 'It is said that the kaṭhina has been withdrawn in that monastery.' For that bhikkhu, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the hearing.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. Tassa bahisīmagatassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsissaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Tassa sā cīvarāsā upacchijjati. Tassa bhikkhuno āsāvacchediko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' To him, having gone outside the boundary, this thought occurs: 'I will attend to this source of hope for a robe right here; I will not return.' He attends to that source of hope for a robe. For him, that hope for a robe is cut off. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is the cutting off of hope.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. So katacīvaro “paccessaṃ paccessa”nti – bahiddhā kathinuddhāraṃ vītināmeti. Tassa bhikkhuno sīmātikkantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. That monk has that robe made. That monk, having a completed robe, thinking, 'I will return, I will return,' lets the time for the kaṭhina withdrawal pass while outside. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the passing of the time limit.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino cīvarāsāya pakkamati “paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Āsāya labhati, anāsāya na labhati. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. So [V 0.0346] katacīvaro “paccessaṃ paccessa”nti – sambhuṇāti kathinuddhāraṃ. Tassa bhikkhuno saha bhikkhūhi kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs with the hope of a robe, thinking, 'I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of hope; he does not obtain it from a source of no hope. That monk has that robe made. That monk, having a completed robe, thinking, 'I will return, I will return,' reaches the withdrawal of the kaṭhina in time. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina occurs together with the other monks.

Āsādoḷasakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Twelve Cases concerning Hope are concluded.

197. Karaṇīyadoḷasakaṃ

197. The Twelve Cases concerning a Duty

320. Bhikkhu [P 1.0262][M 0.0367][T 2.0155] atthatakathino kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamati. Tassa bahisīmagatassa cīvarāsā uppajjati. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Anāsāya labhati, āsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

320. A monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread departs on account of some duty. For that monk, having gone outside the boundary, a hope for a robe arises. He attends to that source of hope for a robe. He obtains it from a source of no hope; he does not obtain it from a source of hope. For him, this thought occurs: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' That monk has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kaṭhina is one that ends with the completion.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamati. Tassa bahisīmagatassa cīvarāsā uppajjati. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Anāsāya labhati, āsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the kathina has been spread departs on account of some duty. For that monk, having gone outside the boundary, a hope for a robe arises. He attends to that hope for a robe. He obtains it from a place where there was no hope; he does not obtain it from a place where there was hope. For him, this thought arises: 'I will not have this robe made; I will not return.' For that monk, the withdrawal of the kathina has its end in determination.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamati. Tassa bahisīmagatassa cīvarāsā uppajjati. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Anāsāya labhati, āsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

For that monk, the withdrawal of the kathina has its end in the loss.

Anāsāya labhati, āsāya [V 0.0347] na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

For that monk, this thought arises: 'I will have this robe made right here.' He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kathina has its end in completion.

For that monk, this thought arises: 'I will have this robe made right here.' He has that robe made. While that robe is being made for him, it is lost. So taṃ cīvarāsaṃ payirupāsati. Anāsāya labhati, āsāya na labhati. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko [P 1.0263] kathinuddhāro.

While he is outside the boundary, a hope for a robe arises. For that monk, this thought arises: 'I will attend to this hope for a robe right here; I will not return.' He attends to that hope for a robe. For him, that hope for a robe is cut off. For that monk, the withdrawal of the kathina is one based on the cutting off of hope.

Karaṇīyadoḷasakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The twelvefold section on duties is concluded.

198. Apavilāyananavakaṃ

198. The Ninefold Section on Not Departing

321. Bhikkhu [T 2.0158] atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ apavilāyamāno apavinayamāno (sī.), apacinayamāno (ka.). Tamenaṃ disaṅgataṃ bhikkhū pucchanti – “kahaṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, vassaṃvuṭṭho, kattha ca te cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukasmiṃ āvāse vassaṃvuṭṭhomhi. Tattha ca me cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “gacchāvuso, taṃ cīvaraṃ āhara, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. So taṃ āvāsaṃ gantvā bhikkhū pucchati – “kahaṃ me, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? Te evaṃ vadanti – “ayaṃ te, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso; kahaṃ gamissasī”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukaṃ nāma amukañca (ka.) āvāsaṃ gamissāmi, tattha me bhikkhū cīvaraṃ karissantī”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “alaṃ, āvuso, mā agamāsi. Mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

321. A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs, desiring his share of the robe-cloth. Monks ask that monk who has gone to another region: “Friend, where did you complete the rains-residence, and in which monastery is your share of the robe-cloth?” He says thus: “I completed the rains-residence in such-and-such a monastery, and my share of the robe-cloth is in that monastery.” They say thus: “Friend, go, bring that robe-cloth; we will make the robe for you right here.” That monk, having gone to that monastery, asks the monks: “Friends, where is my share of the robe-cloth?” They say thus: “Friend, this is your share of the robe-cloth. Where will you go?” He says thus: “I will go to the monastery named so-and-so, and in that monastery, the monks will make my robe.” They say thus: “Friend, enough. Do not go. We will make your robe right here.” To him, this thought occurs: “I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.” He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has completion as its end.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati…pe… “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs… To him, this thought occurs: “I will not have this robe made, nor will I return.” For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has resolution as its end.

Bhikkhu [M 0.0370][V 0.0349] atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati…pe… “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs… To him, this thought occurs: “I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.” He has that robe made. For him, while that robe is being made, it is lost. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has loss as its end.

322. Bhikkhu atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ apavilāyamāno. Tamenaṃ disaṃgataṃ bhikkhū pucchanti – “kahaṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, vassaṃvuṭṭho[T 2.0159], kattha ca te cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukasmiṃ āvāse vassaṃvuṭṭhomhi, tattha ca me cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “gacchāvuso, taṃ cīvaraṃ āhara, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. So taṃ āvāsaṃ gantvā bhikkhū pucchati – “kahaṃ me, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? Te evaṃ vadanti – “ayaṃ te, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ ādāya taṃ āvāsaṃ gacchati. Tamenaṃ antarāmagge bhikkhū pucchanti – “āvuso, kahaṃ gamissasī”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi, tattha me bhikkhū cīvaraṃ karissantī”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “alaṃ, āvuso, mā agamāsi, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa [P 1.0264] bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

322. A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs, desiring his share of the robe-cloth. When he has gone to another region, monks ask him: “Friend, where did you complete the rains-residence, and where is your share of the robe-cloth?” He replies: “I completed the rains-residence in such-and-such a monastery, and my share of the robe-cloth is there.” They say: “Go, friend, bring that robe-cloth; we will make a robe for you here.” He goes to that monastery and asks the monks: “Friends, where is my share of the robe-cloth?” They reply: “Friend, here is your share of the robe-cloth.” He takes that robe-cloth and sets out for that other monastery. On the way, monks ask him: “Friend, where will you go?” He says: “I will go to the monastery named so-and-so, where the monks will make a robe for me.” They say: “Enough, friend, do not go. We will make a robe for you here.” He thinks: “I will have this robe made here and not return.” He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has completion as its end.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ apavilāyamāno. Tamenaṃ disaṃgataṃ bhikkhū pucchanti – “kahaṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, vassaṃvuṭṭho, kattha ca te cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukasmiṃ āvāse vassaṃvuṭṭhomhi, tattha ca me cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “gacchāvuso, taṃ cīvaraṃ āhara, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. So taṃ āvāsaṃ gantvā bhikkhū pucchati – “kahaṃ me, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? Te evaṃ vadanti – “ayaṃ te, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ ādāya taṃ āvāsaṃ gacchati. Tamenaṃ antarāmagge bhikkhū [T 2.0160] pucchanti – “āvuso, kahaṃ gamissasī”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi, tattha me bhikkhū cīvaraṃ karissantī”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “alaṃ, āvuso, mā agamāsi, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs, desiring his share of the robe-cloth. When he has gone to another region, monks ask him: “Friend, where did you complete the rains-residence, and where is your share of the robe-cloth?” He replies: “I completed the rains-residence in such-and-such a monastery, and my share of the robe-cloth is there.” They say: “Go, friend, bring that robe-cloth; we will make a robe for you here.” He goes to that monastery and asks the monks: “Friends, where is my share of the robe-cloth?” They reply: “Friend, here is your share of the robe-cloth.” He takes that robe-cloth and sets out for that other monastery. On the way, monks ask him: “Friend, where will you go?” He says: “I am going to the monastery named so-and-so, where the monks will make a robe for me.” They say: “Enough, friend, do not go. We will make a robe for you here.” He thinks: “I will not have this robe made, and I will not return.” For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has resolution as its end.

Bhikkhu [M 0.0371] atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati…pe… “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti[V 0.0350]. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs… He thinks: “I will have this robe made right here, and I will not return.” He has that robe made. While that robe is being made, it is lost. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has loss as its end.

323. Bhikkhu [T 2.0161] atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ apavilāyamāno. Tamenaṃ disaṃgataṃ bhikkhū pucchanti – “kahaṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, vassaṃvuṭṭho, kattha ca te cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? So evaṃ vadeti – “amukasmiṃ āvāse vassaṃvuṭṭhomhi, tattha ca me cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. Te evaṃ vadanti – “gacchāvuso, taṃ cīvaraṃ āhara, mayaṃ te idha cīvaraṃ karissāmā”ti. So taṃ āvāsaṃ gantvā bhikkhū pucchati – “kahaṃ me, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti? Te evaṃ vadanti – “ayaṃ te, āvuso, cīvarapaṭivīso”ti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ ādāya taṃ āvāsaṃ gacchati. Tassa taṃ āvāsaṃ gatassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

323. A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs, desiring his share of the robe-cloth. When he has gone to another region, monks ask him: “Friend, where did you complete the rains-residence, and where is your share of the robe-cloth?” He says thus: “I completed the rains-residence in such-and-such a monastery, and my share of the robe-cloth is there.” They say thus: “Go, friend, bring that robe-cloth; we will make the robe for you right here.” Having gone to that monastery, he asks the monks: “Friends, where is my share of the robe-cloth?” They say thus: “Friend, this is your share of the robe-cloth.” Taking that robe-cloth, he goes to that other monastery. For him, having arrived at that monastery, this thought occurs: “I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.” He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has completion as its end.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati…pe… “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, desiring to go to another region, departs… The thought occurs: “I will not have this robe made, nor will I return.” For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that has resolution as its end.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino disaṃgamiko pakkamati…pe… “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, intending to go to another region, departs… The thought arises: “I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.” He has that robe made. While that robe is being made for him, it is lost. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that ends with loss.

Apavilāyananavakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Ninefold Section on Desiring is concluded.

199. Phāsuvihārapañcakaṃ

199. The Pentad on Comfortable Abiding

324. Bhikkhu atthatakathino phāsuvihāriko cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamati – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi[T 2.0162], no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati [M 0.0372] vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, paccessa”nti. Tassa bahisīmagatassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ [V 0.0351] cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa bhikkhuno niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

324. A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, abiding comfortably, having taken a robe, departs, thinking: 'I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will return.' For that monk, having gone outside the boundary, this thought arises: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' He has that robe made. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that ends with completion.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino phāsuvihāriko cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamati – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, paccessa”nti. Tassa bahisīmagatassa evaṃ hoti – “nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. Tassa bhikkhuno sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, abiding comfortably, having taken a robe, departs, thinking: 'I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will return.' For that monk, having gone outside the boundary, this thought arises: 'I will not have this robe made, and I will not return.' For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that ends with a decision.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino phāsuvihāriko cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamati – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no [T 2.0163] ce me phāsu bhavissati, paccessa”nti. Tassa bahisīmagatassa evaṃ hoti – “idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa”nti. So taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. Tassa taṃ cīvaraṃ kayiramānaṃ nassati. Tassa bhikkhuno nāsanantiko kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, abiding comfortably, takes a robe and departs, thinking: 'I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will return.' When he has gone outside the boundary, the thought arises: 'I will have this robe made right here; I will not return.' He has that robe made. While that robe is being made for him, it is lost. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that ends with loss.

Bhikkhu atthatakathino phāsuvihāriko cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamati – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. So katacīvaro – “paccessaṃ paccessa”nti bahiddhā kathinuddhāraṃ vītināmeti. Tassa bhikkhuno sīmātikkantiko [P 1.0265] kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, abiding comfortably, takes a robe and departs, thinking: 'I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he has that robe made. Having had the robe made, thinking, 'I will return, I will return,' he lets the time for the withdrawal of the Kathina pass while outside. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina is one that ends with the transgression of the boundary.

Bhikkhu [M 0.0373] atthatakathino phāsuvihāriko cīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamati – “amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce me phāsu bhavissati, amukaṃ nāma āvāsaṃ gamissāmi; tattha me phāsu bhavissati vasissāmi, no ce [V 0.0352] me phāsu bhavissati, paccessa”nti. So bahisīmagato taṃ cīvaraṃ kāreti. So katacīvaro “paccessaṃ paccessa”nti sambhuṇāti kathinuddhāraṃ. Tassa bhikkhuno saha bhikkhūhi kathinuddhāro.

A monk for whom the Kathina has been spread, abiding comfortably, taking a robe, departs, thinking: 'I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will go to a residence named so-and-so; there it will be comfortable for me, and I will stay. If it is not comfortable for me, I will return.' Having gone outside the boundary, he has that robe made. With the robe made, thinking, 'I will return, I will return,' he arrives in time for the withdrawal of the Kathina. For that monk, the withdrawal of the Kathina occurs together with the monks.

Phāsuvihārapañcakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Five on Comfortable Abiding is concluded.

200. Palibodhāpalibodhakathā

200. Discourse on Obstructions and Non-Obstructions

325. Dveme[T 2.0164], bhikkhave, kathinassa palibodhā, dve apalibodhā. Katame ca, bhikkhave, dve kathinassa palibodhā? Āvāsapalibodho ca cīvarapalibodho ca. Kathañca, bhikkhave, āvāsapalibodho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vasati vā tasmiṃ āvāse, sāpekkho vā pakkamati “paccessa”nti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, āvāsapalibodho hoti. Kathañca, bhikkhave, cīvarapalibodho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ akataṃ vā hoti vippakataṃ vā, cīvarāsā vā anupacchinnā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, cīvarapalibodho hoti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, dve kathinassa palibodhā.

325. Monks, there are these two obstructions to the Kathina and two non-obstructions. What, monks, are the two obstructions to the Kathina? The obstruction concerning the residence and the obstruction concerning the robe. And how, monks, is there an obstruction concerning the residence? Here, monks, a monk either dwells in that residence, or departs with attachment, thinking, ‘I will return.’ Thus, monks, there is an obstruction concerning the residence. And how, monks, is there an obstruction concerning the robe? Here, monks, a monk’s robe is either unmade or unfinished, or his hope for a robe has not been cut off. Thus, monks, there is an obstruction concerning the robe. These, monks, are the two obstructions to the Kathina.

Katame ca, bhikkhave, dve kathinassa apalibodhā? Āvāsaapalibodho ca cīvaraapalibodho ca. Kathañca, bhikkhave, āvāsaapalibodho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pakkamati tamhā āvāsā cattena vantena muttena anapekkho anapekkhena (ka.) “na paccessa”nti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, āvāsaapalibodho hoti. Kathañca, bhikkhave, cīvaraapalibodho hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ kataṃ vā hoti, naṭṭhaṃ vā vinaṭṭhaṃ vā daḍḍhaṃ [M 0.0374] vā, cīvarāsā vā upacchinnā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, cīvaraapalibodho hoti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, dve kathinassa apalibodhāti.

And what, monks, are the two non-obstructions of the Kathina? The non-obstruction concerning the residence and the non-obstruction concerning the robe. And how, monks, is there the non-obstruction concerning the residence? Here, monks, a monk departs from that residence, having given it up, having relinquished it, having been released from it, without attachment, thinking, ‘I will not return.’ Thus, monks, there is the non-obstruction concerning the residence. And how, monks, is there the non-obstruction concerning the robe? Here, monks, a monk’s robe is either completed, or ruined, or lost, or burnt, or his hope for a robe is cut off. Thus, monks, there is the non-obstruction concerning the robe. These, monks, are the two non-obstructions of the Kathina.

Palibodhāpalibodhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discourse on obstructions and non-obstructions is concluded.

Kathinakkhandhako niṭṭhito sattamo.

The seventh, the Kathina Chapter, is finished.

201. Tassuddānaṃ

201. The Summary

Tiṃsa [T 2.0165][V 0.0353] pāveyyakā bhikkhū, sāketukkaṇṭhitā vasuṃ;

Vassaṃvuṭṭhokapuṇṇehi, agamuṃ jinadassanaṃ.

Thirty Pāvā bhikkhus, discontented, spent the rains in Sāketa. Having completed the rains-residence, with robes full of rainwater, they went for a sight of the Victor.

Idaṃ vatthu kathinassa, kappissanti ca pañcakā;

Anāmantā asamācārā, tatheva gaṇabhojanaṃ.

This is the basis of the Kathina, and five privileges will be allowable: going without taking leave, going without the complete set of robes, and likewise a group meal.

Yāvadatthañca uppādo, atthatānaṃ bhavissati;

Ñatti evatthatañceva, evañceva anatthataṃ.

Keeping extra robes as required, and the share of robes that arise, will be for those who have spread the Kathina. The formal act, how it is spread, and how it is not spread.

Ullikhi dhovanā ceva, vicāraṇañca chedanaṃ;

Bandhano vaṭṭi kaṇḍusa, daḷhīkammānuvātikā.

Marking, and washing, preparing, and cutting; basting, hemming, stitching the shoulder-covering, strengthening, and adding the lengthwise border.

Paribhaṇḍaṃ [P 1.0266] ovaddheyyaṃ, maddanā nimittaṃ kathā;

Kukku sannidhi nissaggi, na kappaññatra te tayo.

Adding the widthwise border, dyeing it once; cloth obtained by a hint, by indirect speech, borrowed, stored, requiring forfeiture, or without the determination mark—these are not allowable, except for the three robes.

Aññatra pañcātireke, sañchinnena samaṇḍalī;

Nāññatra puggalā sammā, nissīmaṭṭhonumodati.

It is not spread without a robe of five or more sections, without one properly cut and constructed, or without a qualified person; nor if, though properly spread, one outside the boundary gives approval.

Kathinānatthataṃ hoti, evaṃ buddhena desitaṃ;

Ahatākappapiloti, paṃsu pāpaṇikāya ca.

The Kathina is not spread—thus it was taught by the Buddha. New cloth, cloth like new, worn cloth, rag-heap cloth, and cloth from a shop are allowable.

Animittāparikathā, akukku ca asannidhi;

Anissaggi kappakate, tathā ticīvarena ca.

Cloth obtained without a hint, without indirect speech, not borrowed, and not stored; not requiring forfeiture, with the determination mark made, and likewise any of the three robes.

Pañcake vātireke vā, chinne samaṇḍalīkate;

Puggalassatthārā [T 2.0166] sammā, sīmaṭṭho anumodati.

With a robe of five sections or more, properly cut and constructed; by the proper spreading of a qualified person, and with the approval of one within the boundary.

Evaṃ [V 0.0354] kathinattharaṇaṃ, ubbhārassaṭṭhamātikā;

Pakkamananti niṭṭhānaṃ, sanniṭṭhānañca nāsanaṃ.

Thus is the spreading of the Kathina. There are eight headings for its withdrawal: ending with departure, ending with completion, ending with a resolution, and ending with loss.

Savanaṃ [M 0.0375] āsāvacchedi, sīmā sahubbhāraṭṭhamī;

Katacīvaramādāya, “na paccessa”nti gacchati.

The withdrawal ending with hearing, the withdrawal ending with the cutting off of hope, the withdrawal by crossing the boundary, and the withdrawal together with the monks as the eighth. Taking a finished robe, a monk departs thinking, 'I will not return.'

Tassa taṃ kathinuddhārā,e hoti pakkamanantiko;

Ādāya cīvaraṃ yāti, nissīme idaṃ cintayi.

For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina is one that ends with departure. Taking a robe, he goes; outside the boundary, he thinks this:

“Kāressaṃ na paccessa”nti, niṭṭhāne kathinuddhāro;

Ādāya nissīmaṃ neva, “na paccessa”nti mānaso.

"I will get it finished and I will not return." For him, upon its completion, there is the withdrawal of the kathina. Taking it outside the boundary, his thought is, "I will not get it finished, and I will not return."

Tassa taṃ kathinuddhāro, sanniṭṭhānantiko bhave;

Ādāya cīvaraṃ yāti, nissīme idaṃ cintayi.

For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina would be one that ends with a firm decision. Taking a robe, he goes; outside the boundary, he thinks this:

“Kāressaṃ na paccessa”nti, kayiraṃ tassa nassati;

Tassa taṃ kathinuddhāro, bhavati nāsanantiko.

Thinking, "I will get it finished and I will not return," it is lost for him while being made. For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina is one that ends with its loss.

Ādāya yāti “paccessaṃ”, bahi kāreti cīvaraṃ;

Katacīvaro suṇāti, ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ tahiṃ.

A monk takes a robe and departs, thinking, "I will return." He has the robe made outside the boundary. Having finished the robe, he hears that in that monastery the kathina has been withdrawn.

Tassa taṃ kathinuddhāro, bhavati savanantiko;

Ādāya yāti “paccessaṃ”, bahi kāreti cīvaraṃ.

For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina is one that ends with hearing. A monk takes a robe and departs, thinking, "I will return," and has the robe made outside.

Katacīvaro bahiddhā, nāmeti kathinuddhāraṃ;

Tassa taṃ kathinuddhāro, sīmātikkantiko bhave.

The monk who has finished the robe outside lets the time for the kathina withdrawal pass. For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina would be one that ends with the crossing of the time-limit.

Ādāya yāti “paccessaṃ”, bahi kāreti cīvaraṃ;

Katacīvaro [T 2.0167] paccessaṃ, sambhoti kathinuddhāraṃ.

A monk takes a robe and departs, thinking, "I will return," and has the robe made outside. Having finished the robe and intending to return, he is in time for the kathina withdrawal.

Tassa [V 0.0355] taṃ kathinuddhāro, saha bhikkhūhi jāyati;

Ādāya ca samādāya, satta-sattavidhā gati.

For that monk, that withdrawal of the kathina occurs together with the monks. In the cases of 'taking' and 'undertaking,' there are seven variations for each.

Pakkamanantikā natthi, chakke vippakate chaṭṭhe vippakatā (sī.), chaccā vippakathā (ka.) gati;

Ādāya nissīmagataṃ, kāressaṃ iti jāyati.

In the two sets of six, the case ending with departure does not exist. In the case of an unfinished robe, this variation does not exist. The three cases—ending with completion, ending with a firm decision, and ending with loss—arise with the thought, "I will get it finished."

Niṭṭhānaṃ sanniṭṭhānañca, nāsanañca ime tayo;

Ādāya “na paccessa”nti, bahisīme karomiti.

These three—ending with completion, ending with a firm decision, and ending with loss—occur when a monk takes an unfinished robe and departs, thinking, "I will make it outside the boundary, and I will not return."

Niṭṭhānaṃ sanniṭṭhānampi, nāsanampi idaṃ tayo;

Anadhiṭṭhitena nevassa, heṭṭhā tīṇi nayāvidhi.

These three—completion, firm decision, and also loss—apply to that monk only with respect to an undetermined robe. The method for these three is as previously stated.

Ādāya [P 1.0267][M 0.0376] yāti paccessaṃ, bahisīme karomiti;

“Na paccessa”nti kāreti, niṭṭhāne kathinuddhāro.

A monk takes a robe and departs, thinking, "I will return." Then, thinking, "I will make it outside the boundary and I will not return," he has it made. Upon its completion, the withdrawal of the kathina occurs.

Sanniṭṭhānaṃ nāsanañca, savanasīmātikkamā;

Saha bhikkhūhi jāyetha, evaṃ pannarasaṃ gati.

The withdrawals ending with a firm decision, with loss, with hearing, and with crossing the time-limit may occur, as well as the withdrawal together with the monks. Thus, there are fifteen variations.

Samādāya vippakatā, samādāya punā tathā;

Ime te caturo vārā, sabbe pannarasavidhi.

The 'undertaking' section likewise has fifteen variations. Again, the 'taking' and 'undertaking' sections concerning an unfinished robe are similar. All these four sections have fifteen variations each.

Anāsāya ca āsāya, karaṇīyo ca te tayo;

Nayato taṃ vijāneyya, tayo dvādasa dvādasa.

Without expectation and with expectation, and what is to be done—these are the three. One should know them concisely; the three are twelve and twelve.

Apavilānā navettha apavilāyamāneva (syā.), apavinā nava cettha (sī.), phāsu pañcavidhā tahiṃ;

Palibodhāpalibodhā, uddānaṃ nayato katanti.

Herein, there are nine apavilāna sections; therein, comforts are of five kinds. Obstructions and non-obstructions are two. The summary is made concisely. Thus it ends.

Imamhi khandhake vatthū doḷasakapeyyālamukhāni ekasataṃ aṭṭhārasa.

In this chapter, there are one hundred and eighteen topics, for which the three doḷasaka are the introduction to the abbreviated sections.

Kathinakkhandhako niṭṭhito.

The Kathina Khandhaka is concluded.

8. Cīvarakkhandhako

8. The Cīvara Khandhaka

202. Jīvakavatthu

202. The Story of Jīvaka

326. Tena [P 1.0268][M 0.0377][V 0.0356][T 2.0168] samayena buddho bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena vesālī iddhā ceva hoti phitā phītā (bahūsu) ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca; satta ca pāsādasahassāni satta ca pāsādasatāni satta ca pāsādā; satta ca kūṭāgārasahassāni satta ca kūṭāgārasatāni satta ca kūṭāgārāni; satta ca ārāmasahassāni satta ca ārāmasatāni satta ca ārāmā; satta ca pokkharaṇīsahassāni satta ca pokkharaṇīsatāni satta ca pokkharaṇiyo; ambapālī ca gaṇikā abhirūpā hoti dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā, padakkhiṇā padakkhā (syā.) nacce ca gīte ca vādite ca, abhisaṭā atthikānaṃ atthikānaṃ manussānaṃ paññāsāya ca rattiṃ gacchati; tāya ca vesālī bhiyyosomattāya upasobhati. Atha kho rājagahako negamo vesāliṃ agamāsi kenacideva karaṇīyena. Addasā kho rājagahako negamo vesāliṃ iddhañceva phitañca bahujanañca ākiṇṇamanussañca subhikkhañca; satta ca pāsādasahassāni satta ca pāsādasatāni satta ca pāsāde; satta ca kūṭāgārasahassāni satta ca kūṭāgārasatāni satta ca kūṭāgārāni; satta ca ārāmasahassāni satta ca ārāmasatāni satta ca ārāme; satta ca pokkharaṇīsahassāni satta ca pokkharaṇīsatāni satta ca pokkharaṇiyo[T 2.0169]; ambapāliñca gaṇikaṃ abhirūpaṃ dassanīyaṃ pāsādikaṃ paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgataṃ, padakkhiṇaṃ padakkhaṃ (syā.) nacce ca gīte ca vādite ca, abhisaṭaṃ atthikānaṃ atthikānaṃ manussānaṃ paññāsāya ca rattiṃ gacchantiṃ, tāya ca vesāliṃ bhiyyosomattāya upasobhantiṃ.

326. At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing, populous and crowded with people, and had abundant food. There were seven thousand seven hundred and seven mansions, seven thousand seven hundred and seven gabled houses, seven thousand seven hundred and seven parks, and seven thousand seven hundred and seven lotus ponds. And the courtesan Ambapālī was beautiful, lovely, graceful, and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion; she was skilled in dancing, singing, and music. She was sought after by desirous men for a fee of fifty per night. And because of her, Vesālī shone all the more. Then a certain townsman from Rājagaha went to Vesālī on some business. He saw that Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing, populous and crowded with people, and had abundant food. He saw the seven thousand seven hundred and seven mansions, the seven thousand seven hundred and seven gabled houses, the seven thousand seven hundred and seven parks, and the seven thousand seven hundred and seven lotus ponds. He saw the courtesan Ambapālī—beautiful, lovely, graceful, and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion; skilled in dancing, singing, and music; sought after by desirous men for a fee of fifty per night—and he saw that because of her, Vesālī shone all the more.

327. Atha kho rājagahako negamo vesāliyaṃ taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā punadeva rājagahaṃ paccāgañchi. Yena rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ [V 0.0357] seniyaṃ bimbisāraṃ [M 0.0378] etadavoca – “vesālī, deva, iddhā ceva phitā ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca; satta ca pāsādasahassāni…pe… tāya ca vesālī bhiyyosomattāya upasobhati. Sādhu, deva, mayampi gaṇikaṃ vuṭṭhāpessāmā”ti vuṭṭhāpeyyāma (ka.). “Tena hi, bhaṇe, tādisiṃ kumāriṃ jānātha yaṃ tumhe gaṇikaṃ vuṭṭhāpeyyāthā”ti. Tena kho pana samayena rājagahe sālavatī nāma [T 2.0170] kumārī abhirūpā hoti dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā. Atha kho rājagahako negamo sālavatiṃ kumāriṃ gaṇikaṃ [P 1.0269] vuṭṭhāpesi. Atha kho sālavatī gaṇikā nacirasseva padakkhiṇā ahosi nacce ca gīte ca vādite ca, abhisaṭā atthikānaṃ atthikānaṃ manussānaṃ paṭisatena ca rattiṃ gacchati. Atha kho sālavatī gaṇikā nacirasseva gabbhinī ahosi. Atha kho sālavatiyā gaṇikāya etadahosi – “itthī kho gabbhinī purisānaṃ amanāpā. Sace maṃ koci jānissati sālavatī gaṇikā gabbhinīti, sabbo me sakkāro bhañjissati parihāyissati (sī. syā.). Yaṃnūnāhaṃ gilānaṃ paṭivedeyya”nti. Atha kho sālavatī gaṇikā dovārikaṃ āṇāpesi – “mā, bhaṇe dovārika, koci puriso pāvisi. Yo ca maṃ pucchati, ‘gilānā’ti paṭivedehī”ti. “Evaṃ, ayye”ti kho so dovāriko sālavatiyā gaṇikāya paccassosi. Atha kho sālavatī gaṇikā tassa gabbhassa paripākamanvāya puttaṃ vijāyi. Atha kho sālavatī gaṇikā dāsiṃ āṇāpesi – “handa, je, imaṃ dārakaṃ kattarasuppe pakkhipitvā nīharitvā saṅkārakūṭe chaḍḍehī”ti. “Evaṃ, ayye”ti kho sā dāsī sālavatiyā gaṇikāya paṭissutvā taṃ dārakaṃ kattarasuppe pakkhipitvā nīharitvā saṅkārakūṭe chaḍḍesi.

327. Then the townsman from Rājagaha, having completed that business in Vesālī, returned again to Rājagaha. He approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha and said: “Vesālī, sire, is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food. There are seven thousand mansions… and because of her, Vesālī shines all the more. It would be good, sire, if we too were to establish a courtesan.” “Well then, my good man, find such a maiden whom you could establish as a courtesan.” Now at that time, there was a maiden named Sālavatī in Rājagaha who was beautiful, attractive, lovely, and endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. Then the townsman from Rājagaha established the maiden Sālavatī as a courtesan. Before long, Sālavatī the courtesan became skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music; she was sought after by men who desired her, and her price for a night was one hundred. Before long, Sālavatī the courtesan became pregnant. Then this thought occurred to Sālavatī the courtesan: “A pregnant woman is displeasing to men. If anyone finds out that ‘Sālavatī the courtesan is pregnant,’ all my gain will be destroyed. What if I were to announce that I am ill?” Then Sālavatī the courtesan instructed the gatekeeper: “Friend gatekeeper, let no man enter. And whoever asks for me, inform them, ‘She is ill.’” “Yes, madam,” that gatekeeper replied to Sālavatī the courtesan. Then Sālavatī the courtesan, upon the maturing of her pregnancy, gave birth to a son. Then she ordered a female slave: “Now then, girl, place this child in an old winnowing basket, take him out, and discard him on the rubbish heap.” “Yes, madam,” that female slave replied to Sālavatī the courtesan, and having placed the child in an old winnowing basket and taken him out, she discarded him on the rubbish heap.

328. Tena kho pana samayena abhayo nāma rājakumāro kālasseva rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto addasa taṃ dārakaṃ kākehi samparikiṇṇaṃ[T 2.0171], disvāna manusse pucchi – “kiṃ etaṃ, bhaṇe, kākehi samparikiṇṇa”nti? “Dārako, devā”ti. “Jīvati, bhaṇe”ti? “Jīvati, devā”ti. “Tena hi, bhaṇe, taṃ dārakaṃ amhākaṃ antepuraṃ netvā dhātīnaṃ detha posetu”nti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho te manussā abhayassa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā taṃ [M 0.0379] dārakaṃ abhayassa rājakumārassa antepuraṃ netvā dhātīnaṃ adaṃsu – “posethā”ti. Tassa jīvatīti ‘jīvako’ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Kumārena posāpitoti ‘komārabhacco’ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco nacirasseva viññutaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena abhayo rājakumāro tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “kā me, deva, mātā, ko pitā”ti? “Ahampi kho te, bhaṇe jīvaka, mātaraṃ na jānāmi; api cāhaṃ te pitā; mayāsi mayāpi (ka.) posāpito”ti. Atha kho jīvakassa komārabhaccassa etadahosi – “imāni [V 0.0358] kho rājakulāni na sukarāni asippena upajīvituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyya”nti.

328. At that time, Prince Abhaya, while going to attend upon the king early in the morning, saw that boy surrounded by crows. Having seen this, he asked the people, “What is this, friends, surrounded by crows?” “A boy, lord.” “Is he alive, friends?” “He is alive, lord.” “Then, friends, take that boy to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to raise.” “Yes, lord,” those people replied to Prince Abhaya. They took the boy to Prince Abhaya’s inner palace and gave him to the nurses, saying, “Raise him.” Because he was alive, they gave him the name “Jīvaka.” Because he was raised by the prince, they gave him the name “Komārabhacca.” Before long, Jīvaka Komārabhacca became intelligent. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached Prince Abhaya and said this to him, “Who, lord, is my mother, and who is my father?” “I too, friend Jīvaka, do not know your mother. But I am your father; I had you raised.” Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “It is not easy to make a living from these royal families without a skill. What if I were to learn a skill?”

329. Tena kho pana samayena takkasilāyaṃ takkasīlāyaṃ (ka.) disāpāmokkho vejjo paṭivasati. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ anāpucchā yena takkasilā tena [P 1.0270] pakkāmi. Anupubbena yena takkasilā, yena vejjo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ vejjaṃ etadavoca – “icchāmahaṃ, ācariya, sippaṃ sikkhitu”nti. “Tena hi, bhaṇe [T 2.0172] jīvaka, sikkhassū”ti. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco bahuñca gaṇhāti lahuñca gaṇhāti suṭṭhu ca upadhāreti, gahitañcassa na sammussati na pamussati (sī. syā.). Atha kho jīvakassa komārabhaccassa sattannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena etadahosi – “ahaṃ, kho bahuñca gaṇhāmi lahuñca gaṇhāmi suṭṭhu ca upadhāremi, gahitañca me na sammussati, satta ca me vassāni adhīyantassa, nayimassa sippassa anto paññāyati. Kadā imassa sippassa anto paññāyissatī”ti. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena so vejjo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā taṃ vejjaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, ācariya, bahuñca gaṇhāmi lahuñca gaṇhāmi suṭṭhu ca upadhāremi, gahitañca me na sammussati, satta ca me vassāni adhīyantassa, nayimassa sippassa anto paññāyati. Kadā imassa sippassa anto paññāyissatī”ti? “Tena hi, bhaṇe jīvaka, khaṇittiṃ ādāya takkasilāya samantā yojanaṃ āhiṇḍitvā yaṃ kiñci abhesajjaṃ passeyyāsi taṃ āharā”ti. “Evaṃ, ācariyā”ti kho jīvako komārabhacco tassa vejjassa paṭissutvā khaṇittiṃ ādāya takkasilāya [M 0.0380] samantā yojanaṃ āhiṇḍanto na kiñci abhesajjaṃ addasa. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena so vejjo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā taṃ vejjaṃ etadavoca – “āhiṇḍantomhi, ācariya, takkasilāya samantā yojanaṃ, na kiñci āhiṇṭanto na kiñci (ka.) abhesajjaṃ addasa”nti. “Susikkhitosi[T 2.0173], bhaṇe jīvaka. Alaṃ te ettakaṃ jīvikāyā”ti jīvakassa komārabhaccassa parittaṃ pātheyyaṃ pādāsi. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco taṃ parittaṃ pātheyyaṃ ādāya yena rājagahaṃ tena pakkāmi. Atha kho jīvakassa komārabhaccassa taṃ parittaṃ pātheyyaṃ antarāmagge sākete parikkhayaṃ agamāsi. Atha kho jīvakassa komārabhaccassa etadahosi – “ime kho maggā kantārā appodakā appabhakkhā, na sukarā apātheyyena gantuṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ pātheyyaṃ pariyeseyya”nti.

329. At that time, a physician renowned in all directions was residing in Takkasilā. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, without asking permission from Prince Abhaya, set out for Takkasilā. In due course, he went to Takkasilā, to where the physician was, and approached him. Having approached, he said to that physician: “Teacher, I wish to learn the art.” “In that case, friend Jīvaka, you may learn.” Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca learned much and learned quickly, investigated well, and what he had learned was not forgotten by him. Then, after seven years had passed, this thought occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “I learn much and learn quickly, and I investigate well, and what I have learned is not forgotten by me. I have been studying for seven years, yet the end of this art is not apparent. When will the end of this art become apparent?” Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to where that physician was, approached him, and having approached, he said to that physician: “Teacher, I learn much and learn quickly, and I investigate well, and what I have learned is not forgotten by me. I have been studying for seven years, yet the end of this art is not apparent. When will the end of this art become apparent?” “In that case, friend Jīvaka, take a digging tool and, having wandered for a yojana all around Takkasilā, whatever you see that is not medicinal, bring it.” “Very well, teacher,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca replied to that physician in assent. Taking a digging tool and wandering for a yojana all around Takkasilā, he did not see anything that was not medicinal. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to where that physician was, approached him, and having approached, he said to that physician: “Teacher, I have wandered for a yojana all around Takkasilā, and I did not see anything that was not medicinal.” “You are well-trained, friend Jīvaka. This much is enough for your livelihood.” He gave Jīvaka Komārabhacca a small provision for the journey. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking that small provision, set out for Rājagaha. Then, for Jīvaka Komārabhacca, that small provision was exhausted on the way at Sāketa. Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “These roads are a wilderness, with little water and little food; it is not easy to travel without provisions. What if I were to seek provisions?”

Jīvakavatthu niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Story of Jīvaka is finished.

203. Seṭṭhibhariyāvatthu

203. The Story of the Treasurer’s Wife

330. Tena [V 0.0359] kho pana samayena sākete seṭṭhibhariyāya sattavassiko sīsābādho hoti. Bahū mahantā mahantā disāpāmokkhā vejjā āgantvā nāsakkhiṃsu arogaṃ kātuṃ. Bahuṃ hiraññaṃ ādāya agamaṃsu. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco sāketaṃ pavisitvā manusse pucchi – “ko, bhaṇe, gilāno, kaṃ tikicchāmī”ti? “Etissā, ācariya, seṭṭhibhariyāya sattavassiko [P 1.0271] sīsābādho; gaccha, ācariya, seṭṭhibhariyaṃ tikicchāhī”ti. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena seṭṭhissa gahapatissa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā dovārikaṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha, bhaṇe dovārika, seṭṭhibhariyāya pāvada – ‘vejjo, ayye, āgato, so taṃ daṭṭhukāmo’”ti. “Evaṃ, ācariyā”ti kho so dovāriko jīvakassa komārabhaccassa paṭissutvā yena seṭṭhibhariyā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ etadavoca – “vejjo[T 2.0174], ayye, āgato; so taṃ daṭṭhukāmo”ti. “Kīdiso, bhaṇe dovārika, vejjo”ti? “Daharako, ayye”ti. “Alaṃ, bhaṇe dovārika, kiṃ me daharako vejjo karissati? Bahū mahantā mahantā disāpāmokkhā vejjā āgantvā [M 0.0381] nāsakkhiṃsu arogaṃ kātuṃ. Bahuṃ hiraññaṃ ādāya agamaṃsū”ti. Atha kho so dovāriko yena jīvako komārabhacco tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “seṭṭhibhariyā, ācariya, evamāha – ‘alaṃ, bhaṇe dovārika, kiṃ me daharako vejjo karissati? Bahū mahantā mahantā disāpāmokkhā vejjā āgantvā nāsakkhiṃsu arogaṃ kātuṃ. Bahuṃ hiraññaṃ ādāya agamaṃsū’”ti. “Gaccha, bhaṇe dovārika, seṭṭhibhariyāya pāvada – ‘vejjo, ayye, evamāha – mā kira, ayye, pure kiñci adāsi. Yadā arogā ahosi tadā yaṃ iccheyyāsi taṃ dajjeyyāsī’”ti. “Evaṃ, ācariyā”ti kho so dovāriko jīvakassa komārabhaccassa paṭissutvā yena seṭṭhibhariyā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ etadavoca – “vejjo, ayye, evamāha – ‘mā kira, ayye, pure kiñci adāsi. Yadā arogā ahosi tadā yaṃ iccheyyāsi taṃ dajjeyyāsī’”ti. “Tena hi, bhaṇe dovārika, vejjo āgacchatū”ti. “Evaṃ, ayye”ti kho so dovāriko seṭṭhibhariyāya paṭissutvā yena jīvako komārabhacco tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “seṭṭhibhariyā taṃ, ācariya, pakkosatī”ti[T 2.0175].

330. At that time, in Sāketa, the treasurer's wife had a head affliction of seven years' standing. Many great and renowned physicians from all directions came but were unable to effect a cure. Having taken much gold and silver, they departed. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca entered Sāketa and asked the people, 'Who, friends, is ill? Whom shall I treat?' 'Teacher, this treasurer's wife has a head affliction of seven years' standing; go, teacher, and treat the treasurer's wife.' Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the residence of the treasurer, the householder. Having approached, he instructed the gatekeeper, 'Go, friend gatekeeper, and announce to the treasurer's wife: "Madam, a physician has come, and he wishes to see you."' 'Yes, teacher,' the gatekeeper replied to Jīvaka Komārabhacca. He then went to the treasurer's wife and, having approached, said this to her: 'Madam, a physician has come, and he wishes to see you.' 'What sort of physician is he, friend gatekeeper?' 'He is a young man, madam.' 'Enough, friend gatekeeper. What can a young physician do for me? Many great and renowned physicians from all directions came but were unable to effect a cure. Having taken much gold and silver, they departed.' Then the gatekeeper went to Jīvaka Komārabhacca and, having approached, said this to him: 'Teacher, the treasurer's wife says this: "Enough, friend gatekeeper. What can a young physician do for me? Many great and renowned physicians from all directions came but were unable to effect a cure. Having taken much gold and silver, they departed."' 'Go, friend gatekeeper, and announce to the treasurer's wife: "Madam, the physician says this: ‘Do not, madam, give anything beforehand. When you are cured, then you may give what you wish.’"' 'Yes, teacher,' the gatekeeper replied to Jīvaka Komārabhacca. He then went to the treasurer's wife and, having approached, said this to her: 'Madam, the physician says this: "Do not, madam, give anything beforehand. When you are cured, then you may give what you wish."' 'In that case, friend gatekeeper, let the physician come.' 'Yes, madam,' the gatekeeper replied to the treasurer's wife. He then went to Jīvaka Komārabhacca and, having approached, said this to him: 'Teacher, the treasurer's wife summons you.'

Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco yena seṭṭhibhariyā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā seṭṭhibhariyāya vikāraṃ sallakkhetvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ etadavoca – “pasatena, ayye, sappinā attho”ti[V 0.0360]. Atha kho seṭṭhibhariyā jīvakassa komārabhaccassa pasataṃ sappiṃ dāpesi. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco taṃ pasataṃ sappiṃ nānābhesajjehi nippacitvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ mañcake uttānaṃ nipātetvā nipajjāpetvā (sī. syā.) natthuto adāsi. Atha kho taṃ sappiṃ natthuto dinnaṃ mukhato uggañchi. Atha kho seṭṭhibhariyā paṭiggahe niṭṭhubhitvā dāsiṃ āṇāpesi – “handa, je, imaṃ sappiṃ picunā gaṇhāhī”ti. Atha kho jīvakassa komārabhaccassa etadahosi – “acchariyaṃ acchariyaṃ vata bho (syā.) yāva lūkhāyaṃ gharaṇī, yatra hi nāma imaṃ chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ sappiṃ picunā gāhāpessati. Bahukāni [P 1.0272] ca me mahagghāni mahagghāni mahagghāni (sī. syā.) bhesajjāni upagatāni. Kimpi māyaṃ kiñci kañci (syā.) deyyadhammaṃ dassatī”ti. Atha kho seṭṭhibhariyā jīvakassa [M 0.0382] komārabhaccassa vikāraṃ sallakkhetvā jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “kissa tvaṃ, ācariya, vimanosī”ti? Idha me etadahosi – “acchariyaṃ yāva lūkhāyaṃ dharaṇī, yatra hi nāma imaṃ chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ sappiṃ picunā gāhāpessati. Bahukāni ca me mahagghāni sajjāni upagatāni. Kimpi māyaṃ kiñci deyyadhammaṃ dassatī”ti. “Mayaṃ [T 2.0176] kho, ācariya, āgārikā nāma upajānāmetassa saṃyamassa. Varametaṃ sappi dāsānaṃ vā kammakarānaṃ vā pādabbhañjanaṃ vā padīpakaraṇe vā āsittaṃ. Mā kho tvaṃ, ācariya, vimano ahosi. Na te deyyadhammo hāyissatī”ti. Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco seṭṭhibhariyāya sattavassikaṃ sīsābādhaṃ ekeneva natthukammena apakaḍḍhi. Atha kho seṭṭhibhariyā arogā samānā jīvakassa komārabhaccassa cattāri sahassāni pādāsi. Putto – mātā me arogā ṭhitāti cattāri sahassāni pādāsi. Suṇisā – sassu me arogā ṭhitāti cattāri sahassāni pādāsi. Seṭṭhi gahapati – bhariyā me arogā ṭhitāti cattāri sahassāni pādāsi dāsañca dāsiñca assarathañca.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to where the treasurer’s wife was. Having gone, and having observed the treasurer’s wife’s condition, he said this to her: “Madam, there is need of a handful of ghee.” Then the treasurer’s wife had a handful of ghee given to Jīvaka Komārabhacca. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having cooked that handful of ghee with various medicines, and having made the treasurer’s wife lie on her back on a couch, administered it through the nose. Then that ghee, having been administered through the nose, came up from her mouth. Then the treasurer’s wife, having spat into a spittoon, ordered a female servant: “Now, servant, take this ghee with some cotton wool.” Then this thought occurred to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “It is astonishing how frugal this mistress of the house is, that she would have this ghee, which ought to be discarded, taken with cotton wool! And many of my valuable medicines have been used. How will this lady give me any gift at all?” Then the treasurer’s wife, observing Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s change of expression, said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “Teacher, why are you displeased?” “Just now this thought occurred to me: ‘It is astonishing how frugal this mistress of the house is, that she would have this ghee, which ought to be discarded, taken with cotton wool! And many of my valuable medicines have been used. How will this lady give me any gift at all?’” “We, teacher, who are householders, understand the value of economy. It is better that this ghee be used as foot-ointment for the male servants or workers, or be poured for the making of a lamp. Do not be displeased, teacher. Your due gift will not be diminished.” Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca removed the treasurer’s wife’s seven-year head-illness with that single nasal administration. Then the treasurer’s wife, having become well, gave Jīvaka Komārabhacca four thousand. Her son gave four thousand, thinking, “My mother is well.” Her daughter-in-law gave four thousand, thinking, “My mother-in-law is well.” The treasurer householder gave four thousand, thinking, “My wife is well,” and also a male slave, a female slave, and a chariot with horses.

Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco tāni soḷasasahassāni ādāya dāsañca dāsiñca assarathañca yena rājagahaṃ tena pakkāmi. Anupubbena yena rājagahaṃ yena abhayo rājakumāro tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “idaṃ me, deva, paṭhamakammaṃ soḷasasahassāni dāso ca dāsī ca assaratho ca. Paṭiggaṇhātu me devo posāvanika”nti. “Alaṃ, bhaṇe jīvaka; tuyhameva hotu. Amhākaññeva antepure nivesanaṃ māpehī”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho jīvako komārabhacco abhayassa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā abhayassa rājakumārassa antepure nivesanaṃ māpesi.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking those sixteen thousand, a male slave, a female slave, and a horse-chariot, departed for Rājagaha. Proceeding in due course, he went to Rājagaha, to where Prince Abhaya was, and approached him. Having approached, he said this to Prince Abhaya: 'Your Majesty, this is from my first professional act—sixteen thousand, a male slave, a female slave, and a horse-chariot. May Your Majesty accept this as recompense for raising me.' 'Enough, friend Jīvaka; let it be yours alone. Just have a dwelling built in our own inner palace.' 'Very well, Your Majesty,' said Jīvaka Komārabhacca, and having assented to Prince Abhaya, he had a dwelling built in the inner palace of Prince Abhaya.

Seṭṭhibhariyāvatthu niṭṭhitaṃ.

The story of the treasurer's wife is concluded.

204. Bimbisārarājavatthu

204. The Story of King Bimbisāra

331. Tena [T 2.0177][V 0.0361] kho pana samayena rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa bhagandalābādho hoti. Sāṭakā lohitena makkhiyanti. Deviyo disvā uppaṇḍenti – “utunī dāni devo, pupphaṃ devassa uppannaṃ, na ciraṃ nacirasseva (syā.) devo vijāyissatī”ti. Tena rājā maṅku hoti[M 0.0383]. Atha kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ etadavoca – “mayhaṃ kho, bhaṇe abhaya, tādiso ābādho, sāṭakā lohitena makkhiyanti, deviyo maṃ disvā uppaṇḍenti – ‘utunī dāni devo, pupphaṃ devassa uppannaṃ, na ciraṃ devo vijāyissatī’ti. Iṅgha, bhaṇe abhaya, tādisaṃ vejjaṃ jānāhi yo maṃ tikiccheyyā”ti. “Ayaṃ, deva, amhākaṃ jīvako vejjo taruṇo bhadrako. So devaṃ tikicchissatī”ti. “Tena hi, bhaṇe abhaya, jīvakaṃ [P 1.0273] vejjaṃ āṇāpehi; so maṃ tikicchissatī”ti. Atha kho abhayo rājakumāro jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha, bhaṇe jīvaka, rājānaṃ tikicchāhī”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho jīvako komārabhacco abhayassa rājakumārassa paṭissutvā nakhena bhesajjaṃ ādāya yena rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ seniyaṃ bimbisāraṃ etadavoca – “ābādhaṃ te, deva, passāmā”ti passāmīti (syā.). Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa bhagandalābādhaṃ ekeneva ālepena apakaḍḍhi. Atha kho rājā māgadho [T 2.0178] seniyo bimbisāro arogo samāno pañca itthisatāni sabbālaṅkāraṃ bhūsāpetvā omuñcāpetvā puñjaṃ kārāpetvā jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “etaṃ, bhaṇe jīvaka, pañcannaṃ itthisatānaṃ sabbālaṅkāraṃ tuyhaṃ hotū”ti. “Alaṃ, deva, adhikāraṃ me devo saratū”ti. “Tena hi, bhaṇe jīvaka, maṃ upaṭṭhaha, itthāgārañca, buddhappamukhañca bhikkhusaṅgha”nti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho jīvako komārabhacco rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa paccassosi.

331. Now at that time King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had a fistula ailment. His robes were stained with blood. The queens, seeing this, mocked him: “The king is now in his season, the king's flower has bloomed, soon the king will give birth.” The king was embarrassed by this. Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed Prince Abhaya: “My dear Abhaya, I have such an illness—my robes are stained with blood. The queens, seeing me, mock me: ‘The king is now in his season, the king's flower has bloomed, soon the king will give birth.’ Come now, my dear Abhaya, find a physician who can treat me.” “Your Majesty, our physician Jīvaka is young and skilled. He will treat you.” “Then, my dear Abhaya, order the physician Jīvaka; he will treat me.” Then Prince Abhaya ordered Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “Go, dear Jīvaka, treat the king.” “Very well, my lord,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca said in assent to Prince Abhaya. Taking medicine on his fingernail, he approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha. Upon arriving, he said to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha: “Your Majesty, may I examine your ailment?” Then, with a single application, Jīvaka Komārabhacca cured King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha of his fistula ailment. Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, now healthy, had five hundred women adorned with all their ornaments, then had them remove their ornaments and pile them up. He then said to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “Dear Jīvaka, let all these ornaments of the five hundred women be yours.” “Enough, Your Majesty. May the king remember my service.” “Then, dear Jīvaka, attend to me, the women's quarters, and the community of monks headed by the Buddha.” “Very well, Your Majesty,” Jīvaka Komārabhacca assented to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.

Bimbisārarājavatthu niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Story of King Bimbisāra is concluded.

205. Rājagahaseṭṭhivatthu

205. The Story of the Banker of Rājagaha

332. Tena kho pana samayena rājagahakassa seṭṭhissa sattavassiko sīsābādho hoti. Bahū mahantā mahantā disāpāmokkhā vejjā āgantvā nāsakkhiṃsu arogaṃ kātuṃ. Bahuṃ hiraññaṃ ādāya agamaṃsu. Api ca, vejjehi paccakkhāto hoti. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu – “pañcamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatī”ti. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu [V 0.0362] – “sattamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatī”ti. Atha [M 0.0384] kho rājagahakassa negamassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ kho seṭṭhi gahapati bahūpakāro rañño ceva negamassa ca. Api ca, vejjehi paccakkhāto. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu – ‘pañcamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatī’ti. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu – ‘sattamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatī’ti. Ayañca rañño jīvako vejjo taruṇo bhadrako. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ rājānaṃ jīvakaṃ vejjaṃ yāceyyāma seṭṭhiṃ gahapatiṃ [T 2.0179] tikicchitu”nti. Atha kho rājagahako negamo yena rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ seniyaṃ bimbisāraṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, deva, seṭṭhi gahapati bahūpakāro devassa ceva negamassa ca; api ca, vejjehi paccakkhāto. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu – pañcamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatīti. Ekacce vejjā evamāhaṃsu – sattamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatīti. Sādhu devo jīvakaṃ vejjaṃ āṇāpetu seṭṭhiṃ gahapatiṃ tikicchitu”nti[P 1.0274].

332. Now at that time, the banker of Rājagaha had a head disease for seven years. Many great, renowned physicians from various regions came but were unable to cure him. They took much gold and silver and departed. Moreover, he was given up by the physicians. Some physicians said: 'On the fifth day, the banker householder will die.' Others said: 'On the seventh day, the banker householder will die.' Then it occurred to a leading citizen of Rājagaha: 'This banker householder is of great service to both the king and the townspeople. Yet, he has been given up by the physicians. Some physicians say he will die on the fifth day, and others say on the seventh day. And this physician of the king, Jīvaka, is young and skilled. What if we were to request the king to have the physician Jīvaka treat the banker householder?' Then the leading citizen of Rājagaha approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha and said: 'Your Majesty, this banker householder is of great service to Your Majesty and to the townspeople; yet, he has been given up by the physicians. Some say he will die on the fifth day, and others on the seventh. It would be good, Your Majesty, if you would command the physician Jīvaka to treat the banker householder.'

Atha kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha, bhaṇe jīvaka, seṭṭhiṃ gahapatiṃ tikicchāhī”ti. “Evaṃ, devā”ti kho jīvako komārabhacco rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa paṭissutvā yena seṭṭhi gahapati tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā seṭṭhissa gahapatissa vikāraṃ sallakkhetvā seṭṭhiṃ gahapatiṃ etadavoca – “sace tvaṃ, gahapati, arogo bhaveyyāsi sacāhaṃ taṃ gahapati arogāpeyyaṃ (sī.), sacāhaṃ taṃ gahapati arogaṃ kareyyaṃ (syā.) kiṃ me assa deyyadhammo”ti? “Sabbaṃ sāpateyyañca te, ācariya, hotu, ahañca te dāso”ti. “Sakkhissasi pana tvaṃ, gahapati, ekena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti? “Sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, ekena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Sakkhissasi pana tvaṃ, gahapati, dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti? “Sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti[T 2.0180]. “Sakkhissasi pana tvaṃ, gahapati, uttāno sattamāse nipajjitu”nti? “Sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, uttāno sattamāse nipajjitu”nti.

Then the king of Magadha, Seniya Bimbisāra, commanded Jīvaka Komārabhacca, 'Go, my good Jīvaka, and treat the merchant householder.' 'Very well, Your Majesty.' Thus Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having assented to the king of Magadha, Seniya Bimbisāra, went to where the merchant householder was. Having approached, and having observed the merchant householder's affliction, he said this to the merchant householder: 'Householder, if you were to become free from disease, what would be the gift due to me?' 'Teacher, may all my wealth be yours, and may I be your slave.' 'But would you be able, householder, to lie on one side for seven months?' 'I am able, teacher, to lie on one side for seven months.' 'But would you be able, householder, to lie on the second side for seven months?' 'I am able, teacher, to lie on the second side for seven months.' 'But would you be able, householder, to lie supine for seven months?' 'I am able, teacher, to lie supine for seven months.'

Atha kho jīvako komārabhacco seṭṭhiṃ gahapatiṃ mañcake nipātetvā nipajjāpetvā (sī. syā.) mañcake mañcakena (sī.) sambandhitvā sīsacchaviṃ uppāṭetvā phāletvā (sī.) sibbiniṃ vināmetvā dve [M 0.0385] pāṇake nīharitvā mahājanassa dassesi – “passathayye passesyātha (sī.), passatha (syā.), passathayyo (ka.), ime dve pāṇake, ekaṃ khuddakaṃ ekaṃ mahallakaṃ. Ye te ācariyā evamāhaṃsu – pañcamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatīti – tehāyaṃ mahallako pāṇako diṭṭho. Pañcamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhissa gahapatissa matthaluṅgaṃ pariyādiyissati. Matthaluṅgassa pariyādānā seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissati. Sudiṭṭho tehi ācariyehi. Ye te ācariyā evamāhaṃsu – sattamaṃ divasaṃ [V 0.0363] seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissatīti – tehāyaṃ khuddako pāṇako diṭṭho. Sattamaṃ divasaṃ seṭṭhissa gahapatissa matthaluṅgaṃ pariyādiyissati. Matthaluṅgassa pariyādānā seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṃ karissati. Sudiṭṭho tehi ācariyehī”ti. Sibbiniṃ sampaṭipāṭetvā sīsacchaviṃ sibbitvā ālepaṃ adāsi. Atha kho seṭṭhi gahapati sattāhassa accayena jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “nāhaṃ, ācariya, sakkomi ekena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Nanu me tvaṃ, gahapati, paṭissuṇi – sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, ekena passena sattamāse [T 2.0181] nipajjitu”nti? “Saccāhaṃ, ācariya, paṭissuṇiṃ, apāhaṃ marissāmi, nāhaṃ sakkomi ekena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, gahapati, dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjāhī”ti. Atha kho seṭṭhi gahapati sattāhassa accayena jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca [P 1.0275] – “nāhaṃ, ācariya, sakkomi dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Nanu me tvaṃ, gahapati, paṭissuṇi – sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti? “Saccāhaṃ, ācariya, paṭissuṇiṃ, apāhaṃ marissāmi, nāhaṃ, ācariya, sakkomi dutiyena passena sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, gahapati, uttāno sattamāse nipajjāhī”ti. Atha kho seṭṭhi gahapati sattāhassa accayena jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ etadavoca – “nāhaṃ, ācariya, sakkomi uttāno sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Nanu me tvaṃ, gahapati, paṭissuṇi – sakkomahaṃ, ācariya, uttāno sattamāse nipajjitu”nti? “Saccāhaṃ, ācariya, paṭissuṇiṃ, apāhaṃ marissāmi, nāhaṃ sakkomi uttāno sattamāse nipajjitu”nti. “Ahaṃ ce taṃ, gahapati, na vadeyyaṃ, ettakampi tvaṃ na nipajjeyyāsi, api ca paṭikacceva mayā ñāto – tīhi sattāhehi seṭṭhi gahapati arogo bhavissatīti. Uṭṭhehi[M 0.0386], gahapati, arogosi. Jānāsi kiṃ me deyyadhammo”ti? “Sabbaṃ sāpateyyañca te, ācariya, hotu, ahañca te dāso”ti. “Alaṃ, gahapati, mā me [T 2.0182] tvaṃ sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ adāsi, mā ca me dāso. Rañño satasahassaṃ dehi, mayhaṃ satasahassa”nti. Atha kho seṭṭhi gahapati arogo samāno rañño satasahassaṃ adāsi, jīvakassa komārabhaccassa satasahassaṃ.

Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca laid the merchant householder on a couch, fastened him to the couch, cut open the scalp, opened the cranial suture, extracted two creatures, and showed them to the crowd: “See, sirs, these two creatures—one small, one large. Those teachers who said, ‘The merchant householder will die on the fifth day,’—this large creature was seen by them. On the fifth day, the merchant householder’s brain will be consumed. When the brain is consumed, the merchant householder will die. It was well seen by those teachers. Those teachers who said, ‘The merchant householder will die on the seventh day,’—this small creature was seen by them. On the seventh day, the merchant householder’s brain will be consumed. When the brain is consumed, the merchant householder will die. It was well seen by those teachers.” He then repositioned the cranial suture, stitched up the scalp, and applied a salve. After seven days, the merchant householder said to Jīvaka Komārabhacca: “Teacher, I cannot lie on one side for seven months.” “Did you not promise me, householder, saying, ‘I can lie on one side for seven months’?” “It is true, teacher, I promised, but I will die; I cannot lie on one side for seven months.” “Then, householder, lie on the other side for seven months.” After another seven days, the merchant householder said: “Teacher, I cannot lie on the other side for seven months.” “Did you not promise me, householder, saying, ‘I can lie on the other side for seven months’?” “It is true, teacher, I promised, but I will die; I cannot lie on the other side for seven months.” “Then, householder, lie on your back for seven months.” After another seven days, the merchant householder said: “Teacher, I cannot lie on my back for seven months.” “Did you not promise me, householder, saying, ‘I can lie on my back for seven months’?” “It is true, teacher, I promised, but I will die; I cannot lie on my back for seven months.” “If I had not told you this, householder, you would not have lain down for even this long. But I knew from the very beginning: ‘In three weeks, the merchant householder will be well.’ Get up, householder, you are well. Do you know what is due to me?” “All my wealth is yours, teacher, and I am your slave.” “Enough, householder, do not give me all your wealth, and do not be my slave. Give the king a hundred thousand, and give me a hundred thousand.” Then the merchant householder, being well, gave the king a hundred thousand and gave Jīvaka Komārabhacca a hundred thousand.

Rājagahaseṭṭhivatthu niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Story of the Merchant of Rājagaha is concluded.

206. Seṭṭhiputtavatthu

206. The Story of the Merchant's Son

333. Tena kho pana samayena bārāṇaseyyakassa seṭṭhiputtassa mokkhacikāya kīḷantassa antagaṇṭhābādho hoti, yena yāgupi pītā na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, bhattampi bhuttaṃ na sammā [V 0.0364] pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, uccāropi passāvopi na paguṇo. So tena kiso hoti lūkho dubbaṇṇo uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto. Atha kho bārāṇaseyyakassa seṭṭhissa etadahosi – “mayhaṃ kho puttassa tādiso ābādho, yena yāgupi pītā na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, bhattampi bhuttaṃ na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, uccāropi passāvopi na paguṇo. So tena kiso lūkho dubbaṇṇo uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rājagahaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ jīvakaṃ vejjaṃ yāceyyaṃ puttaṃ me tikicchitu”nti. Atha kho bārāṇaseyyako seṭṭhi rājagahaṃ gantvā yena rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ seniyaṃ bimbisāraṃ etadavoca – “mayhaṃ kho, deva, puttassa tādiso ābādho, yena yāgupi pītā na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, bhattampi bhuttaṃ na sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, uccāropi passāvopi na paguṇo.
